name: B4GALT1-CDG (CDG-IId)
aliases: congenital disorder of glycosylation type IId

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A rare type II CDG caused by deficiency of beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase 1, which adds galactose to N-glycan antennae in the Golgi
Reported features include hypotonia, developmental delay and macrocephaly with a Dandy-Walker malformation and hydrocephalus
A coagulopathy with reduced clotting factor activity has been described, in keeping with the CDG spectrum
Myopathy and raised creatine kinase have been noted in reported cases
Transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a type II pattern reflecting loss of terminal galactose
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, including neurosurgical care for hydrocephalus when present
Diagnosis is confirmed by B4GALT1 molecular genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: B4GALT1 encodes a Golgi beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase that transfers galactose onto the N-acetylglucosamine of maturing complex N-glycans. Deficiency leaves glycan antennae lacking terminal galactose, a processing defect that produces a type II transferrin pattern on isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry. Because the enzyme acts after the oligosaccharide has been transferred to protein, the glycans are structurally incomplete rather than absent. Under-galactosylation of numerous glycoproteins is thought to underlie the neurological, coagulation and muscular features.
additionalDifferentials: Other type II CDG subtypes (e.g. MGAT2-CDG, TMEM165-CDG, COG-complex CDG)
Dandy-Walker malformation of other genetic or sporadic cause
Metabolic myopathies with raised creatine kinase
Type I CDGs when the transferrin pattern is ambiguous
additionalInvestigations: Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry showing a type II pattern
Neuroimaging for Dandy-Walker malformation and hydrocephalus
Serum creatine kinase and neuromuscular assessment
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure from hydrocephalus
reference.prognosis: As a very rare disorder, prognosis is defined by a small number of reports; outcome depends on the severity of the brain malformation, hydrocephalus and systemic complications, with variable neurodevelopmental disability. No treatment corrects the enzymatic defect.
pitfalls: Treating the hydrocephalus or malformation without recognising an underlying glycosylation disorder
Not distinguishing type I from type II defects on transferrin analysis
Overlooking the coagulopathy before neurosurgical procedures
Assuming a specific therapy exists when management is supportive
references: Scriver's OMMBID, congenital disorders of glycosylation
Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, disorders of glycosylation
